newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch mourn after second air crash in two months.
newsitem.headline: Dutch mourn after second air crash in two months.

text.p: The Netherlands grieves for the victims of an air crash for the second time in two months, after 32 people died on a pleasure trip when their World War Two vintage Dakota plane crashed into the sea on Wednesday.

Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, returning to Amsterdam from an official visit to Luxembourg, went to comfort relatives of the passengers and crew who had gathered at Schiphol, the home base of the Dutch Dakota Association (DDA) which operated the plane.

It was a grim re-run of his July appearance in Eindhoven when he gave support to the relatives of over 30 young Dutch army bandsmen and women, killed as a Belgian C-130 Hercules transport plane approached the southern Dutch town's airport.
The Netherlands' Queen Beatrix expressed deep shock over the crash, and was said by an official spokesman to have anxiously followed the news as the disaster unwound on Dutch television.
Television pictures showed relatives rushing to Amsterdam's Schiphol airport in a stark reminder of grieving families converging on Eindhoven only nine weeks earlier.
Anne Groeneveld, founder and president of the DDA, appeared shocked as he told a news conference that the task of identifying the victims would start as soon as possible.
"This is a terrible time for us but the worst is for the family members of both the passengers and the crew who have lost their loved ones," he said.
The passengers were reported to be civil servants from the province of North Holland on the return leg of a pleasure trip from Amsterdam to Texel, an island just off the Dutch coast.
All 32 people on the 55-year-old DC-3 Dakota died when it ditched into the North Sea near the naval town of Den Helder at 4.45 p.m. (1445 GMT) after reporting engine trouble.
Eyewitnesses spoke of seeing apparently lifeless bodies still strapped into their seats, drifting in the water.
Coastguard spokesman Pieter Paap said the search and rescue operation around the plane, lodged on a sandbank, had ended and efforts on Thursday would concentrate on recovering wreckage.
Groeneveld said the plane, used for mainly for air displays and pleasure trips, was in perfect technical condition and had recently been checked by the national civil aviation authority.
His organisation is a band of pilots and aviation enthusiasts who bought the DC-3 in 1983 for 300,000 guilders ($160,000) and lovingly restored it to its former glory.
